title: $1.50 and Five Girls. Now It's a University.

brand.cta: Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

beats.text: She started a school with a dollar fifty.
Born in South Carolina in 1875 to formerly enslaved parents, she was picking cotton by age nine.
She became a teacher. In 1904, in Daytona, Florida, she rented a small house and opened her own school.
She had a dollar fifty. Her first students were five little girls, and her son.
In two years, she had two hundred and fifty students.

visual.caption: Bethune with the college choir, Daytona Beach, 1943

beats.text: It merged with a men's college to become Bethune-Cookman. She led it for decades.

visual.caption: Bethune in her office at Bethune-Cookman College, 1943

beats.text: In 1935, she founded the National Council of Negro Women. Then Roosevelt brought her into his government.
She led his informal Black Cabinet, and befriended Eleanor Roosevelt.
In 1945, she was the only Black woman at the founding of the United Nations.
She died in 1955. In 2022, she became the first Black American with a state statue in the Capitol.
A dollar fifty and five girls. Now: Bethune-Cookman University.

facts.claim: Born 10 July 1875 near Mayesville, SC; one of the last (15th) of 17 children of formerly enslaved parents; picked 250 lb of cotton a day by age 9.
October 1904, rented a house in Daytona and opened a school for Black girls.
Opened with $1.50 and five girls (plus her son).
In less than two years, 250 students.
Merged with Cookman Institute (1923-1929; sources differ) to form Bethune-Cookman; president until 1942.
Founded the National Council of Negro Women in 1935; National Youth Administration 1936.
Leader of FDR's informal 'Black Cabinet'; close friend of Eleanor Roosevelt.
Only Black woman / woman of colour at the 1945 founding conference of the UN.
Died 1955; July 2022 first African American with a state statue in National Statuary Hall.

notUsed: Exact merger year (1923, 1925, 1929, 1931 depending on the step)
